intro.text: Three jobs on one starter. Each starts with a report. You choose the tests and say what you expect. Then read the meter. Name the fault and prove it fixed. Theory turns up when a reading surprises you.

jobs.title: No click
jobs.report: Report: Pump 2 won't start from the panel. No click from the starter. The overload hasn't tripped.

route.thought: The break is in the top half: the fuse, the panel Stop or the pump's Stop loop.
Fuse and panel Stop are whole. It's in the pump's Stop loop.
The Stop is fine, so a core is open.
The core out to the pump is open.

jobs.title: The Stop that won't stop
jobs.report: Report: Pump 2's cable was damaged and joined yesterday. Now the Stop at the pump doesn't stop it. The panel Stop does.

route.thought: Both cores sit in one connector. The pump's Stop is joined out.
Held pressed, it still reads near zero. Something bridges it.

jobs.title: After a contactor change
jobs.report: Report: The contactor on Pump 2 was changed yesterday. Now it buzzes when Start is pressed, and the pump won't run.

route.thought: The circuit feeds the coil from one line and neutral, so 230 V. This coil wants 400 V.
Your fix worked, but the job isn't done.
Terminal 14 is empty. The hold-in wire was never moved across.

notes.title: What keeps the coil fed
notes.words: Press Start and current reaches the coil through the button. The coil pulls in the main contacts. A small hold-in contact, wired across Start, closes with them. Let go and Start springs open. Now the coil is fed through the hold-in contact instead. If that contact or its wires are open, the coil drops out the moment you let go.

notes.title: Split it in half
notes.words: Six places could hold the break. Test across the top three. Whichever way it reads, you've cleared three. Test across half of what's left and you're down to one or two. Piece by piece can take five tests. Halving takes three at most.

notes.title: A healthy open contact
notes.words: Start is normally open. Dead, with nobody pressing it, it reads over range even when it's perfect. Hold it in, or use the toggle, before you call it faulty. The hold-in contact is open too while the contactor is out.

notes.title: Test it the way it's used
notes.words: A Stop is normally closed, so it reads near zero at rest. That proves it closes, not that it opens. Hold it pressed and test again. A healthy Stop now reads over range. Near zero means something bridges it.

notes.title: The right voltage for the wrong coil
notes.words: The circuit feeds the coil from one line and neutral, so it gets 230 V. That's only healthy if the coil is rated 230 V. This one is rated 400 V, so it gets about 58% of its rating. A coil is made to pull in within a band, for example 85% to 110% of its rating. Below it, the armature can't seat fully, so it buzzes.

notes.title: What a dead reading means
notes.words: A whole wire or a closed contact reads near zero. A break reads over range. So does a healthy normally open contact, unless it is held in. The coil reads in between.

screens.text: Three jobs on one starter. Each starts with a report. You choose the tests and say what you expect. Then read the meter. Name the fault and prove it fixed. Theory turns up when a reading surprises you.
Quick one first. Pump 2 runs only while someone holds Start. Let go and it stops. What do you check?

options.slip: A tripped overload stops it pulling in at all. Here it pulls in.

options.text: The hold-in contact and its wire
options.why: Yes. The coil pulls in, so its whole path works. Only the path that keeps it fed after Start springs back is in doubt.

options.slip: The coil pulls in while Start is held. It works.
The motor runs while Start is held. The fault is in what keeps it running.

options.text: Isolate, then test along the coil's circuit
options.why: Yes. No click means the coil never pulled in. Find where its path is broken, dead.

options.text: Reset the overload and try again
options.slip: The flag shows no trip. There's nothing to reset.
Nothing points at the coil yet. Swapping parts before testing is guessing.
No click means the contactor never closed. The motor isn't reached yet.

screens.text: Tap every part that could cause this.

options.text: Stop at the pump and its cable

screens.after: Anything in the coil's path could. The hold-in contact can't, because with Start held it plays no part. The overload flag makes a trip unlikely, but its contact or wires could still be open.

screens.text: Before you touch a terminal, make it dead and prove it. Put the steps in order.
screens.after: That's the order. A tester that fails can show dead on a live circuit, so prove it before and after.

options.why: Good. A dead test will find an open circuit, so there's no reason to work live.

options.text: Leave it live and trace the voltage
options.slip: Accidents often happen in fault-finding, when there's pressure to get plant running. The law allows live work only when it's unreasonable for the circuit to be dead. Here a dead continuity test will find it, so working live can't be justified. Isolate instead?

screens.text: Pick a test and two points. Say what you expect, then read it.
screens.hint: Try a test that clears half of what's left, whichever way it reads.

screens.text: Where is the break, and what is it?

options.why: Yes. The core out to the pump's Stop is open. The Stop itself reads near zero.

options.slip: Nothing here joins two wires that should be apart.
Every part is the one that was there before.
It reads over range, not a little high.

review.text: P0 to P3 over range. P0 to P2 near zero. R1 to R2 near zero. P2 to R1 over range. Where is the break?

screens.text: You're on your own for this one.
Start: it pulls in and runs. Let go: it stops. Your fix worked, but the job isn't done.

review.text: You fitted the right coil. Start, let go, and it stops. Where now?

b1.q: A new AB on your section asks why Pump 2 buzzed, and why it still wouldn't keep running after you fixed that. Tell them in a few plain sentences.

points.text: The buzz meant the coil was getting power.
A 400 V coil fed 230 V can't pull in fully. It gets about 58% of its rating, below its band.
Then the hold-in wire hadn't been moved to the new contactor, so it stopped when Start was let go.
After any change, prove start, hold and every Stop.
Plain words a new hand would follow.

b1.model: It buzzed, so the coil was getting power. But the new coil was rated 400 V, and this circuit feeds it 230 V from one line and neutral. That's too little for it to pull in, so it buzzed. With a 230 V coil fitted, it ran only while Start was held. The hold-in wire had never been moved to the new contactor. Always prove start, hold and every Stop after a change.

keep.title: The pump that won't run
keep.for: Finding why a DOL starter won't start, won't stop or won't hold.
keep.rule:
Make it safe, then start with what changed.
No click, overload not tripped: split the coil's path in half, dead.
Test a contact the way it's used: Start held in, Stop held pressed.
Runs only while Start is held: the hold-in contact or its wire.
Buzzes: read the coil's rating, then how it's fed.
After any control repair, prove start, hold and every Stop.

traps.text: A healthy Start reads open. A bridged Stop reads closed, just like a healthy one.
230 V at the coil is only right for a 230 V coil.
One fix can hide a second fault.

keep.where: Any DOL starter: pumps, fans and compressors.
